readings.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 49, a. 2 (Whether the supreme good, God, is the cause of evil)
readings.note: Read the article for the distinction between the evil that is fault and the evil that is penalty, and for the argument that the order of the universe requires things that can fail. A thirteenth-century theological argument, not a magisterial act; it is the clearest statement of one legitimate line of response.

readings.title: Spe Salvi 35–37 (Benedict XVI, 2007)
readings.note: Read the section on action and suffering as settings for learning hope, including the double claim that we must fight suffering and cannot eliminate it, and the account of healing not by fleeing suffering but through accepting it and finding meaning in union with Christ. An encyclical: authoritative teaching, and explicitly a meditation rather than a definition.

visual.title: What is defined, what is disputed, and what cannot be answered
visual.description: A three-band diagram of Catholic teaching on suffering, with the pastoral rule for each band.
steps: Defined: God is good and not the cause of moral evil (CCC 311); evil entered through creaturely freedom; God can bring good from evil's consequences (CCC 312)
Defined: no quick answer, and the full account awaits the end (CCC 309, 314); not every suffering is a punishment or a fault (SD 11; John 9:3; Job 42:7)
Disputed among legitimate responses: the free-will argument, the order of the universe, the redemptive meaning of suffering with Christ, the eschatological deferral, and educative accounts
Permitted and excluded practice: accompany, pray, help; do not announce God's particular intention, do not claim an outcome is guaranteed, do not explain anyone's pain
Pastoral rule from the psalter: lament is prayer, and Psalm 88 ends in darkness without resolution

lessons.title: Science, faith, and how to read a question the Church has not settled
lessons.explanation: Objective: learn a five-step procedure for reading a contested question, and apply it to the case that generated the largest literature, the relation of Catholic teaching to the natural sciences. The procedure is: state the question; sort the claims by kind; establish what the Church has defined, what she has taught non-definitively, and what she has left open; identify which disciplines have competence; and state what evidence would change your mind. The Church's own texts on science do the sorting for us. The First Vatican Council's distinction, quoted in Fides et Ratio 9, is that “there exists a twofold order of knowledge, distinct not only as regards their source, but also as regards their object”: we know one by natural reason and the other by divine faith, and neither is identical with nor opposed to the other. Gaudium et Spes 36 draws the practical consequence: if methodical investigation is carried out in a genuinely scientific manner and in accord with moral norms, “it never truly conflicts with faith, for earthly matters and the concerns of faith derive from the same God,” and the same council affirms “the legitimate autonomy of human culture and especially of the sciences” (GS 59). Fides et Ratio 49 adds the limit that matters most for this lesson: “The Church has no philosophy of her own nor does she canonize any one particular philosophy in preference to others” — the magisterium is not a scientific or philosophical academy, and when it intervenes in those fields its competence has a purpose (guarding the faith) rather than an expertise it does not claim. Leo XIII had already stated the boundary for Scripture: the sacred writers “did not seek to penetrate the secrets of nature, but rather described and dealt with things in more or less figurative language, or in terms which were commonly used at the time” (Providentissimus Deus 18), a point the Catechism restates when it says that scientific study of origins has “splendidly enriched our knowledge” and prompts greater admiration for the Creator (CCC 283). The case then becomes testable. On human origins the Church has a non-definitive intervention that constrains: Pius XII's Humani Generis 37 held that the faithful “cannot embrace that opinion” which maintains that after Adam there existed true human beings not descended from him, or that Adam represents a number of first parents, because it seemed irreconcilable with the doctrine of original sin as transmitted from one. The International Theological Commission's 2004 study accepts the science as science — noting that converging evidence from physical and biological sciences “furnishes mounting support for some theory of evolution,” and that anthropology and molecular biology make a convincing case for human origins in Africa in a population of common lineage — and simultaneously quotes John Paul II's 1996 message calling evolution “more than a hypothesis” while insisting that the message is not “a blanket approbation of all theories of evolution,” since materialist readings are excluded and the “ontological leap” to the human person cannot be explained in purely scientific terms (Communion and Stewardship 63–64).
lessons.example: Apply the five steps to the question: does Catholic teaching conflict with evolutionary science? Step one, state the question precisely. “Does the Church deny evolution?” is not one question but four: is the universe and life old and developing; are human beings biologically descended from earlier populations; is there a single first human couple; and is the human person reducible to biology. Step two, sort the claims. The first is empirical biology, geology, and cosmology. The second is empirical biology with a theological entailment. The third is empirical with a doctrinal entailment. The fourth is philosophical and theological, and no scientific finding settles it. Step three, establish the Church's position by kind. The compatibility of faith with methodical science is taught and stable (GS 36, GS 59, CCC 159, CCC 283). The age and development of life are not doctrinal questions at all. The unity of the human race, in the sense required by the transmission of original sin and the claim that all share one nature, is a doctrinal commitment; Humani Generis 37 stated a constraint on one formulation of polygenism, and it did so as a warning about reconcilability rather than as a definition, which is why it belongs in the third category this course examined in lesson 31. Step four, competence: cosmology, palaeontology, and genetics are not the magisterium's to decide; the identity of the human person as image of God is not the sciences' to decide, which is why the commission speaks of an ontological leap rather than a gap to be closed later by data. Step five, what would change your mind. If a magisterial document claimed that Scripture teaches a six-day chronology, that would be a doctrinal claim in tension with the observable record, and one would have to ask what kind of act it was. If a scientific finding purported to show that human beings are not a single species, that would bear on a premise of the doctrine of original sin's transmission, and it would be a problem for theology rather than a proof that the doctrine is false. Notice that both sentences are about the relation between kinds of claim, not about who is winning.
lessons.question: A student concludes from Humani Generis 37 that the Church has defined monogenism and rejected all evolutionary accounts of human origins. Which assessment is accurate?
lessons.answer: Humani Generis 37 is authoritative teaching that warned against a particular polygenist formulation as difficult to reconcile with the doctrine of original sin; it is not a definition, it did not reject evolutionary accounts as such, and the International Theological Commission's 2004 study shows later theological work accepting the science while defending the person's unique status.
lessons.distractor: The Church has defined monogenism, so any Catholic who accepts mainstream human evolutionary biology is in conflict with defined doctrine.
lessons.correction: The document confines itself to saying that the faithful “cannot embrace” the specified opinion because of the difficulty of reconciling it with the transmission of original sin, which is a statement about reconciliation rather than a definition of the human genealogy; the passage of time has also changed the scientific picture the question is about. The commission's study demonstrates the Church's own recognition that the theological question continues to be worked out. Reading this as a definition would be the exact error lesson 31 taught: treating non-definitive teaching either as dogma or as nothing.

depth.definitions: The twofold order of knowledge, quoted at Fides et Ratio 9 from the First Vatican Council, distinguishes truths known by natural reason from truths held by divine faith, distinct in source and object. Legitimate autonomy of the sciences means that disciplines have their own principles and methods and are not adjudicated by theology (GS 59). Magisterial competence concerns faith and morals; an intervention in philosophy or science is directed to protecting the faith, which is why Fides et Ratio 49 denies that the Church has a philosophy of her own. Monogenism is the claim of descent from a single first couple; polygenism its denial; the ITC study treats the scientific evidence for a common ancestral population as strong while reserving the theological question. An ontological leap is the commission's phrase for the difference between a highly developed animal life and a person, which it says “cannot be explained in purely scientific terms.” Concordism is the error of forcing Scripture and science into a single framework of explanation; fideism leaves faith unargued; scientism treats the methods of natural science as the only route to truth, which Gaudium et Spes 59 and Fides et Ratio both reject.
depth.mechanism: The five-step procedure works because most disputed questions are bundles: an empirical claim, a philosophical claim, and a theological claim travelling together under one headline. Separating them does three things. It tells you which literature to read: the biology of human origins is read in journals, the doctrine of original sin in Trent and the Catechism, and the relation between them in the International Theological Commission, not in any of the three. It tells you who has competence, which matters because an intervention by the Church in a question of fact is a different kind of act from a definition of faith, and because an intervention by a scientist in a question of meaning is a different kind of act from a discovery. And it protects against the two symmetrical errors that make this topic so unproductive: using a religious text as a scientific hypothesis, and using a scientific method as a complete philosophy. The commission's own language models the discipline: it cites the 1996 message approvingly and then immediately limits what the message can be taken to say, which is precisely the reading discipline practised throughout this level. Two further rules are worth stating. First, ask about the date. A text written before a scientific development cannot be read as though it had that development in view; Humani Generis was written before the molecular evidence for human origins existed, and its argument is about reconcilability with a doctrine, not about genetics. Second, ask about the object. A definition about the person's creation in God's image is an answer to a question about nature and destiny, and no measurement of gene frequencies answers or refutes it.
depth.secondExample: Test the procedure on a case where the Church's own record contains a correction: the treatment of Galileo. The history is well known — the condemnation of heliocentrism in the seventeenth century — and the question is what kind of act it was and what follows. Read the Church's own use of the episode. Fides et Ratio's note 29 quotes John Paul II's 1979 address to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, where he recalled that Galileo had grasped that the two truths of faith and science can never contradict each other, and the note immediately observes that the Second Vatican Council says the same thing in similar language in Gaudium et Spes 36. Two things follow, and they pull in the same direction. First, the episode shows that a non-doctrinal judgement by ecclesiastical authority can be mistaken and can later be revised; the Church's own citation of it as an illustration of harmony presupposes that the earlier intervention is not a permanent claim on the faith. Second, it shows the limit of the lesson: the corrections that matter in this area concern judgements about how Scripture relates to the natural world, and the discipline of Providentissimus Deus 18 — that Scripture does not teach the structure of the physical universe — is the principle that prevents the repetition. Note that Catholic teaching does not claim infallibility for disciplinary or prudential acts, and the notion of a “dogmatic fact,” which lesson 31 examined, concerns facts bound up with doctrine, not every historical judgement a churchman has made. A student who says the Church was simply wrong about astronomy and a student who says the Church never erred are both skipping the question of what kind of act the 1633 decision was.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first is concordism, reading Genesis as a physical narrative and then defending or attacking it as such; both moves duplicate the error Providentissimus Deus 18 identified. The second is scientism, treating a method's success in its own domain as a licence to pronounce on meaning and value, which the same conciliar texts exclude from the other direction. The third is treating every magisterial intervention as if it had the same weight, which means a warning about reconcilability in 1950 is read as a definition and a definition is read as a policy preference. The fourth, and the one this lesson most wants to prevent, is the false resolution: answering a genuinely contested question — here, how the doctrine of original sin is to be articulated given what is known about human ancestry — by declaring either that the Church has settled it or that the Church has been disproved. The Church has not settled it, which is why the International Theological Commission published a study rather than a definition, and the study is the evidence for that claim. A teacher who reports the state of the question accurately, including the fact that it remains open, has done the job; a teacher who awards a victory to either side has left the subject.
depth.application: Optional capstone: choose one contested question and produce a five-section briefing using the procedure of this lesson. Section one: the question in one sentence, with the bundle unpacked into its empirical, philosophical, doctrinal, and prudential parts. Section two: for each part, what the Church has defined, what she has taught non-definitively, and what is open, with a located citation or an explicit statement that nothing is found. Section three: which disciplines are competent, and which kinds of evidence decide each part. Section four: the strongest argument available to each of two positions you have not adopted, stated so that a holder would recognise it. Section five: what evidence would change your own mind, and what you would refuse to claim in the meantime. Model entry for section two on human origins: defined — the person is created in God's image and destined for communion with God; taught non-definitively — the warning of Humani Generis 37 about the reconciliation of polygenism with original sin; open — the theological articulation of original sin given the scientific account of a common ancestral population, which the International Theological Commission treats as work in progress. Self-review rubric: every claim assigned to a category with a reason; at least one item marked as open; no position attributed to a source that does not hold it; a stated condition under which the writer would revise.
depth.summary: Sort the claims, establish the Church's position by kind rather than by headline, name the competent disciplines, and say what would change your mind: that is how a contested question is read without pretending it is settled. Applied to science, the procedure shows a stable teaching about the two orders of knowledge, a non-definitive intervention about human origins whose scope is narrower than either side reports, and a live theological question that the Church's own commission treats as open. This completes a level that has moved from praying, through reading and worship, to living with others and with unanswered questions — and it leaves the student with the discipline that makes the whole course usable: name the act, state the claim, and never claim more than the sources do.

readings.title: Gaudium et Spes 36 and 59 (1965)
readings.note: Read 36 for the claim that methodical investigation carried out in a genuinely scientific manner does not conflict with faith, and 59 for the legitimate autonomy of culture and the sciences. Conciliar text; paragraph numbers locate each claim.

readings.title: Fides et Ratio 9 and 49 (John Paul II, 1998), with note 29 on Galileo
readings.note: Read 9 for the twofold order of knowledge quoted from the First Vatican Council, 49 for the statement that the Church has no philosophy of her own and does not canonise one, and the notes for the citation of John Paul II's 1979 address to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences on Galileo and the cross-reference to Gaudium et Spes 36. An encyclical: authoritative teaching in an argumentative mode.

readings.title: Humani Generis 36–37 (Pius XII, 1950)
readings.note: Read the passage cautioning against treating the bodily origin of man from living matter as proved, then the paragraph stating that the faithful cannot embrace the specified polygenist opinion because of the difficulty of reconciling it with the transmission of original sin. Note the vocabulary: a warning about reconciliation, not a definition — the distinction lesson 31 established.

visual.title: Five steps for a contested question, applied to science and faith
visual.description: A procedure diagram with the science-and-faith case filled in at each step.
steps: Step 1 — state the question, unpacking the bundle: age of the universe; human descent; a single first couple; the person as more than biology
Step 2 — sort the claims: empirical, philosophical, doctrinal, prudential
Step 3 — establish the Church's position by kind: taught (GS 36, 59; CCC 159, 283); non-definitive (Humani Generis 37); open (the articulation of original sin given human ancestry)

Step 4 — name the competent disciplines: cosmology, palaeontology, and genetics decide the first three parts; theology and philosophy decide the fourth; Fides et Ratio 49 denies that the Church has a philosophy of her own to impose
Step 5 — state what would change your mind, and say plainly which parts of the question remain unsettled

questions.prompt: A columnist argues that because a particular moral teaching is not infallibly defined, Catholics may set it aside whenever they judge it mistaken, and adds that following one's conscience settles the matter. Which correction follows from the Church's own document on dissent?
questions.answer: Non-definitive teaching calls for religious submission of will and intellect, and conscience cannot legitimate public rejection of a teaching because conscience must itself be formed and is not an autonomous authority for deciding the truth of a doctrine.
questions.distractor: The columnist is right, since the Church distinguishes only between infallible definitions and private opinions, and everything else is a matter for individual judgement.
questions.correction: Donum Veritatis 33 names and rejects that dichotomy as a kind of theological positivism, and 38 states that conscience “is not an independent and infallible faculty” while conceding the believer's obligation to follow a formed conscience. The legitimate space for argument lies in examining arguments, raising difficulties with the magisterium, and criticising prudential judgements, not in declaring the teaching void.

questions.prompt: Two local congregations plan a joint eucharistic celebration as a visible sign of growing unity, and a third proposes instead a shared service of evening prayer, a joint food drive, and a study circle on the Lord's Prayer. Which assessment matches the Church's rules?
questions.answer: The shared liturgy is not permitted because eucharistic communion presupposes full communion in faith, sacraments, and governance, whereas the shared prayer, cooperation, and study are appropriate ecumenical activity, with conversion of heart as its condition.
questions.distractor: Both are permitted, because shared baptism establishes sufficient communion for any form of joint worship including the Eucharist.
questions.correction: Ecclesia de Eucharistia 44 states the rule and its reason, and distinguishes concelebration from the administration of the sacraments to individuals in grave need (n. 45; CCC 1401). Unitatis Redintegratio 7 supplies the condition that makes the rest of the activity real: there can be no ecumenism worthy of the name without a change of heart.

questions.prompt: A parish interreligious committee proposes a joint day of service with a local mosque, followed by a shared meal at which a member of each community explains how their tradition understands almsgiving. A parishioner objects that any such event denies that Christ is the only Saviour. How should the objection be handled?
questions.answer: The event enacts the forms of dialogue of action and of religious experience that the Church's own document names, while the objection misidentifies it: the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions and still proclaims Christ as the only mediator, and the theological question of how the traditions stand in God's plan is not settled by the event.
questions.distractor: The objection is correct, because Nostra Aetate permits only academic dialogue and not common action with members of other religions.
questions.correction: Dialogue and Proclamation 42 lists four forms — life, action, theological exchange, and religious experience — and 43 explicitly warns against reducing dialogue to the specialist form. Nostra Aetate 2 holds recognition and uniqueness together in one sentence, and CCC 846–848 states the doctrinal limits. The correction is not to cancel the event but to state the Church's teaching inside it.

questions.prompt: A retreat speaker tells participants that anyone who suffers greatly must have unconfessed sin in their life, because God blesses the faithful and disciplines the guilty. Which texts should a catechist bring to the discussion?
questions.answer: John 9:3, where Jesus refuses the question of whose sin caused a man's blindness; Job 42:7, where God says Job's friends have not spoken rightly; and Salvifici Doloris 11, which states that it is not true that all suffering is a consequence of a fault.
questions.distractor: Only the Book of Proverbs, since the wisdom literature teaches a reliable correspondence between virtue and prosperity in this life.
questions.correction: The claim is the mechanical reading the sources reject. The Catechism adds the doctrinal frame: God is in no way the cause of moral evil (CCC 311), God can bring good from evil's consequences (CCC 312), and the full account awaits the end (CCC 314). Note also that the psalter itself contains prayer that does not resolve, as in Psalm 88's closing line.

questions.prompt: A school board asks whether a Catholic biology syllabus may teach the scientific account of human origins. One member cites Humani Generis 37 as forbidding it; another cites the International Theological Commission's 2004 study. How should the question be resolved?
questions.answer: Sort the claims: the scientific account of human ancestry is an empirical matter outside magisterial competence, the warning in Humani Generis 37 concerns the reconcilability of one polygenist formulation with the transmission of original sin and is not a definition, and the theological articulation of original sin given human ancestry is a question the Church's own commission treats as still under discussion.
questions.distractor: Neither source is relevant, because the Church has never addressed the relation between faith and the natural sciences and therefore has no teaching on the matter.
questions.correction: The relation is addressed in the Church's teaching: Gaudium et Spes 36 states that methodical investigation carried out in a genuinely scientific manner never truly conflicts with faith, GS 59 affirms the legitimate autonomy of the sciences, Fides et Ratio 49 denies that the Church has a philosophy of her own, and Providentissimus Deus 18 had already distinguished Scripture's purpose from the investigation of nature. The commission's study is the evidence that a theological question remains open rather than settled in either direction.

questions.prompt: A widely forwarded message states that scientists have now proved that prayer has no effect, and that a separate study has proved that a particular novena always works. Assess both claims using this level's categories and state what a careful reader would say instead.
questions.answer: Both claims assert more than their evidence can carry and both misdescribe the kind of question at issue: prayer is presented in the Church's teaching as a real address to a personal God whose action is not a measurable quantity reducible to a controlled outcome, and no source promises a guaranteed result from a devotional practice; a careful reader would separate the empirical question about measurable effects, which research may address, from the theological claim about God's freedom and about petition as an appointed means.
questions.distractor: The first claim is sound and the second is merely an overstatement, since a controlled study of intercessory prayer settles what the Church has always claimed about petition.
questions.correction: The category error is the same in both directions: a statistical result and a devotional guarantee both treat God's action as a mechanism. The Catechism holds gift and effort together (CCC 2725) and describes petition within trust rather than technique (CCC 2736); Aquinas is explicit that prayer does not change the divine disposition (ST II–II, q. 83, a. 2). Measurable psychological effects of practice are a legitimate research question and are not the same question as whether God hears.

questions.prompt: A homilist builds a doctrinal claim on three quotations: a sentence from Psalm 14 that reads “There is no God,” a proverb that he attributes to Scripture in the words “money is the root of all evil,” and the sentence “the letter brings death” offered as a warning against biblical scholarship. Identify the failure mode of each and state the repair, and explain why the repairs are not interchangeable.
questions.answer: The first is a fragment — the sentence belongs to the fool the psalm refutes, repaired by locating the speaker and the argument; the second is a misquote — the text names the love of money, repaired by collating a citable edition; the third is a severed verse — 2 Corinthians 3 contrasts the ministries of the old and new covenants, repaired by reading the unit of argument, with the whole reading disciplined by the three criteria of Dei Verbum 12.
questions.distractor: All three are examples of the same error, the misuse of figurative language, and all are repaired in the same way, by consulting the Church's teaching instead of the text.
questions.correction: Each failure mode requires its own repair because each has a different cause: ignorance of a text's internal speakers, inaccurate transmission, and loss of context. CCC 116 supplies the governing rule that all other senses rest on the literal sense, so an appeal to a spiritual reading cannot repair a literal-level error; and using the Church's teaching as a substitute for reading the text is the very move the criteria of Dei Verbum 12 constrain rather than license.

questions.prompt: A diocesan office proposes three changes together: introducing a locally composed eucharistic prayer, moving the sign of peace to before the offertory in all parishes, and shortening the homily. A liturgist objects that the first is a doctrinal issue, the second is a matter of taste, and the third is inadmissible because the Church's law regulates preaching. Assess all four statements.
questions.answer: The first proposal does touch the substance of the sacrament, since the eucharistic prayer is not a matter of local composition; the second is a legitimate question of competence rather than of doctrine, since the position of the sign of peace is regulated and the competent authority can decide it; the third is a prudential and pastoral matter rather than a legal absolute; and the liturgist's own classification is therefore wrong twice.
questions.distractor: All three proposals are matters of discipline that the competent authority may freely decide, because the Church distinguishes only between doctrine and law and everything in a liturgy is law.
questions.correction: SC 22 §3 rules out individual change, and CCC 1125 rules out arbitrary change even by the supreme authority, while CCC 1205 distinguishes the immutable part of the liturgy from the parts the Church may adapt. Proposals must therefore be sorted by stratum rather than merged: the composition of the eucharistic prayer concerns the substance received from Christ; the placement of a rite is regulation; the length of a homily is pastoral judgement. The liturgist has applied the labels without the criterion.

questions.prompt: A catechist prepares a lesson arguing that the Council of Trent invented the doctrine of the Eucharist because the Middle Ages had turned the Mass into an abuse, and supports it with a quotation from a devotional book that says the sacrament is “a symbol of Christ's presence, received spiritually by the faithful.” Assess both the argument and the quotation.
questions.answer: The argument confuses the date of a technical formulation with the date of a belief, since the early witnesses attest a realism that excludes a merely symbolic reading and Trent presents the conversion as a belief already firm in the Church which the council declares anew; the quotation, by contrast, states a position that Trent's definition excludes, since the chapter claims the conversion of the whole substance rather than a sign.
questions.distractor: The argument is sound because historical abuses explain the origin of doctrines, and the quotation is harmless because it uses the word received rather than a technical term.
questions.correction: Two distinct errors should be separated: a historical claim about origins, which the early texts refute on the specific point of realism, and a doctrinal claim in the devotional book, which contradicts the definition rather than merely reverting to an older vocabulary. Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 7, and Justin, First Apology 66, are the early evidence; Trent XIII ch. IV is the definition; CCC 1374–1375 is the synthesis.

questions.prompt: A Catholic voters' guide claims the Church requires support for one economic programme because Pope Leo XIII condemned socialism, and a rival guide claims the Church requires the opposite because the same pope defended private property. Set out how a reader should assess both guides and what a Catholic is actually obliged to do.
questions.answer: Both guides extract a single element from an argument whose parts were held together — the condemnation of a proposal to abolish property and the insistence that the earth is destined for all — and then convert a prudential conclusion into a required policy; a Catholic is obliged to accept the principles, to exclude policies that the principles themselves rule out, and to form and defend a prudential judgement on the basis of evidence.
questions.distractor: At least one guide must be right, because a papal encyclical states the Church's teaching and the Church's teaching determines which policies a Catholic may support.
questions.correction: Rerum Novarum argues both against the abolition of private property and against the wage relations of its own day (nn. 4–8), which is the pattern the tradition continues: the four permanent principles are interlocking (Compendium n. 160), subsidy must help rather than absorb (Quadragesimo Anno 79), and Paul VI explicitly declines to propose a solution of universal validity (Octogesima Adveniens 4). What is not optional is the exclusion of policies that deny human dignity or treat labour as a commodity.

questions.prompt: A theologian and a bishop disagree publicly over a non-definitive moral teaching. The theologian has published a book setting out arguments against it and clearly stating that she proposes a revision; the bishop has written a pastoral letter explaining the teaching and asking for assent. A journalist reports that a theological dispute proves the teaching is now optional. Untangle the three positions.
questions.answer: The theologian's book, if it presents difficulties with an argument and does not claim to represent the Church, is the activity Donum Veritatis treats as a service to the Church; the bishop's letter states the teaching and requests the assent owed to non-definitive teaching; and the journalist's inference is precisely the position the same declaration rejects, since contestation in public or in scholarship does not make a teaching optional.
questions.distractor: Because the theologian's arguments are public and the bishop's letter is only pastoral, the teaching has become a private matter on which Catholics may hold either opinion.
questions.correction: Distinguish the act from the forum: private or scholarly presentation of difficulties is distinguished from public opposition to a teaching (DV 32), the freedom of the act of faith does not create a right to dissent (DV 36), and conscience cannot legitimate dissent since it must be formed and is not an autonomous authority for the truth of a doctrine (DV 38). Meanwhile CCC 1785, 1790, and lesson 31's categories keep the two obligations — follow a certain conscience, and form it — in view at once.

questions.prompt: A parish representative asks the bishop for permission for a joint eucharistic liturgy with an Orthodox congregation, on the ground that the Orthodox possess true sacraments, and separately asks whether members of a neighbouring Protestant congregation may receive communion at a Catholic Mass. Advise on both questions and give the reason in each case.
questions.answer: The joint liturgy may not be held: concelebration requires full communion in faith, sacraments, and governance, and the absence of full communion with the Orthodox concerns the primacy and other questions, not the validity of their sacraments; individual members of the Protestant congregation may in principle receive the sacraments in grave necessity under the conditions the Church specifies, which require that they ask of their own accord, hold the Catholic faith regarding the sacrament, and be properly disposed.
questions.distractor: Both requests should be refused, because sacraments may never be given to anyone outside full communion, and the fact that a community lacks valid orders is irrelevant to the question.
questions.correction: The two questions turn on different distinctions. Validity explains why the Orthodox possess true sacraments and therefore why their situation differs from that of communities that have not preserved a valid episcopate (CCC 1399–1400; Dominus Iesus 17); the bonds of communion explain why concelebration is nevertheless not possible (Ecclesia de Eucharistia 44); and the pastoral exception for individuals in grave need is stated with its conditions at Ecclesia de Eucharistia 45–46 and CCC 1401. Refusing to distinguish them produces the very indifferentism, or the very rigidity, that this level's lessons warn against.

questions.prompt: A Catholic teacher is asked, in front of a class that includes Muslim and Jewish students, whether their religions are paths of salvation. Set out the answer a teacher could give that is both faithful to the Church's teaching and honest about what is not settled.
questions.answer: The teacher should state what the Church teaches — that God wills the salvation of all, that all grace is Christ's and Christ is the unique mediator, that the Church is necessary to salvation in the sense her teaching defines, and that the affirmation is not aimed at those who through no fault of their own do not know Christ; should note that the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions and rejects discrimination on religious grounds; and should say plainly that how the religious traditions themselves stand in God's plan is a question the council did not settle and Catholic theologians still debate.
questions.distractor: The teacher should affirm that all religions are equally valid paths to God, since Nostra Aetate praises what is true and holy in them, and should leave the question of Christ's uniqueness unaddressed as a private matter.
questions.correction: The two errors excluded are equivalent and symmetrical: treating the traditions as alternative paths contradicts Dominus Iesus 13–14 and CCC 846–848, and treating them as simply false contradicts Nostra Aetate 2. The honest answer distinguishes the doctrinal commitments from the open theological question, which is the same discipline the class will need for every other contested question — and the teacher should be able to say which part of the answer is defined and which is a live discussion among theologians.

questions.prompt: A funeral homilist says that the deceased's long illness was God's way of preparing her for heaven, that her family's prayers had failed because they lacked faith, and that the appropriate Christian response is simply to accept the mystery. Assess each of the three statements.
questions.answer: The first attributes to God a particular intention the sources do not support, since God is not the cause of moral evil and the disciples' causal question in John 9 was refused; the second is excluded by the teaching that no procedure obliges God and by the refusal to treat suffering as a verdict on the sufferer; the third is right about the limit of knowledge and wrong if it is used to silence grief, since the psalter itself prays lament in unresolved terms.
questions.distractor: All three statements are acceptable, because in the face of death the Church permits any sincere words of consolation and forbids no formulation.
questions.correction: The three statements have different defects: an over-claim about God's particular intention, an assertion that converts prayer into a mechanism and blames the bereaved, and a true claim misapplied. The sources are specific — CCC 311 and 314 set the limits, SD 11 and John 9:3 refuse the causal reading, Psalm 88 shows a lament that ends in darkness, and SD 19 makes the positive claim that suffering can be united with Christ's. The pastoral rule from the lesson is to answer the question actually asked, and not to explain what the Church does not claim to know.

questions.prompt: A student writing a paper on faith and science asserts that the Church has condemned evolution, that Pius XII defined monogenism, and that the Church's teaching on creation is therefore a scientific hypothesis vulnerable to disproof. Rebuild the paper's argument correctly using the sources.
questions.answer: The Church's teaching distinguishes two orders of knowledge and affirms the legitimate autonomy of the sciences, so she has not condemned evolutionary science; Pius XII's 1950 warning concerned the reconcilability of one polygenist formulation with the doctrine of original sin and is not a definition; and creation in God's image is a claim about the person's origin and destiny that no measurement addresses, which is why the International Theological Commission could accept the scientific account of human ancestry while holding the theological question open.
questions.distractor: The assertions should be retained with minor corrections, since the Church has in fact attempted to define scientific questions and the appropriate response is to defend those definitions against contrary evidence.
questions.correction: Three errors are packed into the three assertions: a false historical claim, a category error about the weight of a non-definitive intervention, and a methodological error that treats a claim about meaning as an empirical hypothesis. The correcting sources are Gaudium et Spes 36 and 59, Fides et Ratio 9 and 49, Providentissimus Deus 18, Humani Generis 37, and Communion and Stewardship 63–65, with CCC 159 and 283 supplying the Catechism's synthetic statement.

questions.prompt: You are asked to write a single-page briefing for a parish council on a disputed question it must discuss next week — the question is the council's choice, but the briefing must be usable whether the council is arguing about liturgy, about a social policy, or about interreligious relations. Set out the sequence of moves your briefing will make and justify the order.
questions.answer: Identify the question and unpack the bundle of claims it contains; classify each claim as empirical, philosophical, doctrinal, or prudential; locate what the Church has defined, what she has taught non-definitively, and what she has left open, citing by locator and using the criteria of document, insistence, and manner of expression; identify which authority and which disciplines have competence; state the strongest version of the position you do not hold; and state plainly which parts of the question remain unsettled and what evidence would change your mind.
questions.distractor: Quote the most authoritative-sounding sentence available from whatever document addresses the topic, treat it as the Church's answer, and arrange the remaining material as supporting commentary.
questions.correction: The order matters because each step constrains the next. Unpacking the bundle prevents a headline from deciding a question that contains four different questions; classification fixes the weight and the forum; the three-category analysis prevents both inflation and dismissal of teaching (lesson 31); competence tells you which literature to read and which arguments are simply in the wrong domain; stating the opposing position honestly is the test of whether you have understood the question; and naming what is open is the only way to avoid claiming more than the sources claim. A briefing that begins from the conclusion has given up every one of those constraints.

questions.prompt: A diocese's adult-education committee wants one session that teaches Catholics how to respond when a neighbour or a family member brings them a disputed religious claim — a supposed promise attached to a devotion, a proof-text, an assertion that the Church has changed its teaching, or an accusation that Catholics worship Mary. Design the single organising principle of the session and apply it to one of the four claims.
questions.answer: The organising principle is a fixed sequence of questions: what kind of act or claim is this; what does it actually say in its own setting; what has the Church defined, taught non-definitively, or left open, and where; and what may therefore be claimed or refused. Applied to the claimed promise in a devotion, the sequence yields: the claim is a devotional assertion with no magisterial standing; the Church's teaching is that petition belongs to a relationship of trust and that no procedure obliges God (CCC 2626–2649, 2736; ST II–II, q. 83, a. 2); the practice itself may be legitimate and even encouraged when it does not carry a guarantee, since the Church regulates popular piety rather than suppressing it.
questions.distractor: The organising principle should be to identify the Church's teaching on the topic and present it as the answer, since Catholics need clear positions rather than questions about the standing of claims.
questions.correction: Clear positions are the result of the sequence, not a substitute for it: a Catholic who can only recite conclusions cannot answer the next variant of the claim, and will either inflate a devotion into a doctrine or dismiss an authoritative teaching as opinion. The method is the one this level has built — classify the act (lessons 31, 34, 43), read the text in its own setting (lessons 33, 42, 44), locate what is defined and what is not (lessons 35, 45, 46, 47, 48, 50), and refuse to claim what the sources do not (lessons 40, 41, 49). Applied to the other three claims it produces the same shape: a fragment repaired by context, a claimed change tested by asking what kind of act changed, and a doctrinal objection answered by the distinction between worship and veneration.
